Task","minutes":5,"standards":["W.6.2"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Listen as your teacher explains your essay. Then turn to a partner and name one myth from this unit that you might write about."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"You have read myths from many cultures. Now you will write an explanatory essay showing what these stories teach us about being human, how they explain the world, and how they express values."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"You have two choices. You can compare two myths that share a similar lesson or theme, or you can classify several myths into types, such as creation, hero, cautionary, or transformation. Either way, you will also create a visual, like a chart, concept map, or digital collage, to help your reader see your thinking."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"At the end of the unit you will use your essay in a seminar or podcast. You will listen, respond to classmates, and connect ideas to modern values. Today we plan so that tomorrow we can write with confidence."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which myth from this unit has stuck with you, and what did it teach?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The story of Arachne stuck with me because she was too proud and got turned into a spider. It taught that bragging can get you in trouble."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to five minutes. Students need only one myth in mind. Have the unit's myth list posted so students who struggle to recall can pick from it."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Rehearse complex thesis statements with although, while and because, and build precise comparative vocabulary and pronoun clarity.","activities":[{"id":"lab-thesis-rehearsal","title":"Building and Rehearsing a Thesis","minutes":10,"standards":["W.6.2.a","W.6.2.d","W.6.5"],"routine":"Sentence Combining","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Students combine short ideas about two myths into one thesis using subordinating conjunctions, then say the thesis aloud before writing. Use myths your class has read; the example below is a placeholder, so swap in a pair from your unit if you like."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"A strong thesis does more than name two myths. It tells the reader how they connect. Let's combine short ideas into one sentence. Read these kernel sentences."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Display: Myth A explains why the seasons change. Myth B explains why the seasons change. The cultures give different reasons. Both stories show people trying to understand nature."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Here is a combined thesis: Although the Greek myth of Persephone and a creation story from another culture come from different places, both show that people used stories to explain nature because they wanted to make sense of a mysterious world. Notice although shows a contrast, both shows a similarity, and because gives a reason."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which word shows how the myths are different, and which shows how they are alike?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Although shows they are different because they come from different places. Both shows they are alike because they both explain nature."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Comparative language helps your reader follow. Use similarly, both, and like to show likeness. Use unlike, while, and in contrast to show difference. Watch your pronouns too. If you write they, make sure the reader knows which myths they means. Say the myth names, or write the first myth and the second myth."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"This sentence says, It teaches that pride is dangerous, but the other one says it is okay. What is unclear?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It and the other one do not tell which myth we mean. I would write Arachne's story teaches that pride is dangerous, while the myth of Narcissus suggests that self-love can trap a person."},{"type":"directions","text":"Write a one-sentence thesis for your essay. Use although, while, or because. If you are classifying, name the category and the myths in it. Then say your thesis aloud to a partner, and have your partner point out any pronoun that is unclear."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Listen for theses that only list myths. Prompt: Add although, while, or because to show how they connect. Students will refine this thesis later in the Research Essay Outline."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: writing a thesis with a subordinating conjunction","tryThis":"Give the frames: Although ___ and ___ are different, both show ___. While ___ teaches ___, ___ shows ___. Let students say the sentence aloud first and then write it."},{"situation":"Struggling with: pronoun clarity","tryThis":"Have students circle every it, they, or this and write the myth name above it. Replace the pronoun if the reader cannot tell what it points to."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to write two thesis options, one comparing and one classifying, and choose the stronger one with a reason."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Use a model essay to define success, then plan the essay and visual with the Research Essay Outline.","activities":[{"id":"lia-model-essay","title":"Study the Model Essay","minutes":10,"standards":["W.6.2","W.6.2.a","SL.6.5"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"Model explanatory essay: comparing or classifying myths","pages":"Entire model"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read the model essay. Annotate the thesis, one transition, one comparative word, one piece of evidence from each myth, and the visual. Then share with a partner."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A successful essay has six parts. A clear thesis names a shared theme or category. Logical organization uses transitions that show relationships. Precise comparative language uses words like both, unlike, while, and although. Relevant evidence comes from more than one myth. A visual such as a chart, concept map, or digital collage helps the reader see your reasoning. And the style is formal."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Where does the model essay state its thesis, and what does it promise to explain?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The thesis is in the introduction. It promises to explain how the myths share the same lesson even though they come from different cultures."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the visual help the reader that the paragraphs alone might not?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The chart puts the two myths side by side, so you can quickly see what is the same and what is different without reading everything again."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["W.6.2.a"],"stem":"According to the success criteria, what is the main job of the visual in the essay?","choices":[{"text":"To help the reader see the reasoning behind the comparison or categories","correct":true,"rationale":"The visual should make the comparison or classification easier to see and understand."},{"text":"To make the essay look more colorful","correct":false,"rationale":"Decoration alone does not help the reader understand the ideas."},{"text":"To replace the paragraphs so students write less","correct":false,"rationale":"The visual supports the writing; it does not replace it."},{"text":"To retell each myth from beginning to end","correct":false,"rationale":"Retelling is not the purpose; the visual shows the relationships between myths."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Students read a model closely and name its features using comparative language.","sayAsk":"Say: Point to a word that shows two things are alike. Ask: Which words show a difference? Frames: Both ___ and ___ show ___. ___ is different from ___ because ___. The visual shows ___. Before annotating, have students preview the model with a partner and say what the two myths are.","watchFor":"If students annotate every sentence, then prompt: Mark only the six features. If students cannot find the thesis, then prompt: Look for the sentence that names the shared theme. Success: students label at least four features and explain one aloud."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding essay features in the model","tryThis":"Give a checklist with the six features and have students match one highlighted example to each. Read the model aloud once before annotating."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to find one place where the model could use a stronger transition or more precise comparison and rewrite it."}]}]},{"id":"lia-plan-outline","title":"Plan the Essay and Visual","minutes":20,"standards":["W.6.2","W.6.2.a","W.6.5","W.6.8","SL.6.5"],"routine":"Independent Planning with Partner Check","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Use your annotations and notes on this unit's myths to choose your myths. Decide whether you will compare two myths or classify several. Then fill in the Research Essay Outline with your thesis, body paragraphs, evidence, transitions, conclusion, and visual plan."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"I am looking at my notes. I have annotations on several myths, but I cannot use everything. I ask which myths share a lesson I can explain with strong evidence. Then I write my thesis in the outline and decide what each paragraph will prove. If I classify, each body paragraph can be one type of myth. If I compare, I can organize by similarity and difference."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Evidence needs to come from your notes on more than one myth. Use a quotation or a paraphrase, and note which text it came from so you can credit it. Write in your own words so you do not copy. Check that each source you use is a myth you actually read in this unit."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What will your visual show, and where will it fit in your essay?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I will make a two-column chart comparing the lessons, the characters, and the reasons each myth was told. It will go after my second paragraph so the reader can see what I just explained."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How will you make sure your transitions show relationships between the myths?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I will use similarly when the myths agree and in contrast when they differ, so the reader knows how each paragraph connects to my thesis."},{"type":"directions","text":"Partner check: Read your thesis and paragraph plan aloud. Your partner answers: Does the evidence match the thesis? Is there a visual that helps? Revise one part of your outline based on the feedback."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Circulate with the thesis rubric items: shared theme or category, evidence from two or more myths, visual, transitions. Confer first with students who have not picked myths. Students who plan a digital collage should note image sources they might use."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Students plan with adverbials and comparative language to add detail about how, when, and why myths are alike and different.","sayAsk":"Say: Add a detail about why or how. Ask: What do both myths explain? Frames: Both myths explain ___ by telling ___. In the first myth, ___; however, in the second myth, ___. For example, ___. Students rehearse each paragraph orally before writing notes.","watchFor":"If students list facts without connecting them, then prompt: Add while or in contrast to show the relationship. If students use only one myth for evidence, then prompt: Find a matching detail from the second myth. Success: the outline has evidence from two myths and a transition in each paragraph."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: choosing myths or a structure","tryThis":"Offer a short list of paired myths from the unit and a simple structure: introduction, similarity, difference, visual, conclusion. Let students tell a partner why the myths go together before writing."},{"situation":"Struggling with: planning the visual","tryThis":"Provide a sample two-column chart and sentence frame: My visual shows ___. It helps the reader see ___."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to plan a connection to a modern value for the seminar or podcast, such as honesty or humility, and note which myth supports it."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Reflect on the plan and set a next step toward drafting.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-quick-write","title":"Quick Write: Readiness to Draft","minutes":5,"standards":["W.6.5","W.6.2"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Write your response to the question."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How ready is your essay plan, and what is one thing you still need to do?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"My plan is almost ready. I have a thesis that uses although and two myths with evidence. I still need to finish my visual idea and add a transition for my conclusion."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Optional sentence starter: My plan is strong because ___. My next step is ___."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework","purpose":"Finish the essay outline (optional).","activities":[{"id":"homework-finish-outline","title":"Finish the Essay Outline","minutes":0,"standards":["W.6.5"],"routine":"Independent work","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Finish your Research Essay Outline. Make sure it includes your thesis, evidence from at least two myths, transitions, and a plan for your visual. Bring it to the next lesson so you can begin drafting."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students learn the Shared Stories, Shared Lessons essay task, study a model essay, and rehearse complex thesis statements with although, while and because. They then plan an explanatory essay and visual that compare or classify myths from different cultures using the Research Essay Outline.","keyActivities":["Launch: introduce the compare-or-classify essay and the seminar or podcast","Literacy Lab: sentence combining and oral rehearsal of thesis statements, comparative language, pronoun clarity","Model essay annotation to identify success criteria","Independent planning in the Research Essay Outline with partner check","Quick Write on readiness to draft"],"vocabularyTaught":["thesis","classify","theme","comparative language","transition","myth","visual"],"standardsCovered":["W.6.2","W.6.2.a","W.6.5","W.6.8","SL.6.5","W.6.2.d"]}}
